title: Pieces of April
full_review:
"Pieces of April" (MGM) is a bittersweet dramedy about a young woman whose attempt at reconciliation with her estranged family by hosting Thanksgiving dinner is jeopardized when she discovers her stove has decided to take a holiday. While at first glance the simple premise appears not to have enough narrative stuffing to prove engaging, director Peter Hedges elicits good performances from his ensemble cast, serving up an emotionally satisfying feast.

Katie Holmes plays April Burns, a bohemian free spirit living in a dilapidated, racially diverse tenement in New York City's Lower East Side. At the prompting of her good-hearted, live-in boyfriend, Bobby (Derek Luke), April extends an olive branch to her parents, agreeing to take on turkey duty in the hope of mending her broken relationship with her cancer-stricken mother, Joy (Patricia Clarkson).

On the other end of the emotional wishbone is April's dad, Jim (Oliver Platt), who desperately wants the day -- perhaps the last Thanksgiving they will share together as a family -- to be a happy memory for Joy.

With Bobby out on an errand and her parents, along with good daughter Beth (Alison Pill), brother Timmy (John Gallagher Jr.) and senile grandma Dottie (Alice Drummond) on the way, April learns that her oven is broke. Racing against time, April begins to go door-to-door, bird in tow, searching for a working stove, striking up friendships with neighbors who up until this point had been strangers, including Eugene and Evette (Isaiah Whitlock and Lillias White), a generous African-American couple, and a Chinese family who proves that kindness transcends language.

Paralleling April's culinary conundrum is the Burnses' car ride into the city, darkened by Joy's growing apprehension of what will likely unfold when they reach their destination, fearing that the day will end -- as it usually does when she and April are in the same ZIP code -- in conflict. Their story hits one moral speed bump on the road down during a scene in which mother and son share a joint -- though its disagreeableness may be diminished for some viewers given Joy's medical condition and marijuana's alleged therapeutic use as an effective painkiller.

On a much more positive note, "Pieces of April" imparts a poignant message about love and forgiveness, using the celebration of a meal as a poetic -- almost sacramental -- symbol of the sacred bond shared by family members. Likewise, the solidarity displayed by the neighbors pitching in to help cook April's turkey beautifully illustrates the Christian teaching concerning the basic human need for community.

This spirit of interdependence is given expression during a scene in which April attempts to explain Thanksgiving to her non-English-speaking Chinese neighbors by teaching them about the Pilgrims and Indians, offering the syrupy yet meaningful observation, "There came a day when they knew they needed each other, when they knew they couldn't do it alone."

Having lost his own mother to cancer, Hedges' insights concerning the fleetingness of life serve as eloquent reminders to cherish the time we have to share with each other as a precious gift.
Though well-written, many of this modest film's most potent moments unfold without words; they include a scene in a roadside diner's restroom and the movie's emotional payoff, rendered through a montage of still photographs.

Due to some rough and crude language, a few instances of profanity, a scene involving marijuana, as well as some images of nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
